## Original idea
{
  "title": "CRADE: Joint Contamination-Ability Decomposition via Gated Item Response Theory with Paired Adversarial Items",
  "core_problem": "No existing framework can determine whether a model fails adversarial benchmark variants because it memorized original answers (contamination) or because it lacks genuine reasoning ability (capability deficit) — all current work observes this entanglement but none models it within a measurement-theoretic framework, preventing trustworthy LLM capability assessment.",
  "opportunity": "Three previously siloed research streams — IRT-based LLM evaluation (PSN-IRT AAAI 2026 Oral, ATLAS, LEGO-IRT), contamination detection/correction (DCR EMNLP 2025, ConStat NeurIPS 2024, JECS arXiv May 2026), and adversarial robustness testing (MaSTer, RIDE, MATH-Perturb ICML 2025) — have each matured independently to the point where their integration is both technically feasible and urgently needed. The critical catalyst is Wang et al.'s ICLR 2026 proof that all likelihood-based contamination detection fails on reasoning models (AUROC ≈ 50%), creating demand for response-pattern-based alternatives that bypass token-probability signals entirely. A key theoretical precedent exists but has never been applied to LLMs: the Deterministic Gated IRT model (DGM; Shu, Henson & Luecht, Psychometrika 2013) decomposes test performance into genuine ability and cheating/preknowledge components conditioned on item exposure status — precisely the structure needed for LLM contamination. PSN-IRT showed IRT works for LLMs (12 models, 41,871 items, 4PL) but left contamination-adjusted scoring as an explicit open question, flagging anomalous guessing-rate parameters as contamination indicators without providing corrected ability estimates. RankLLM (ICLR 2026) demonstrated that non-parametric difficulty-aware ranking achieves 90% human alignment with only a damping hyperparameter — but provides no contamination decomposition, producing rankings without interpretable ability vs. memorization parameters. The AAAI 2027 deadline (abstracts July 21, papers July 28, 2026) is 8 weeks out. Nobody sits at the three-way intersection of IRT estimation, contamination correction, and adversarial pairing because these communities publish at different venues (ACL/EMNLP for contamination, ICLR/NeurIPS for robustness, AAAI for psychometric evaluation, Psychometrika/JEBS for test security).",
  "landscape": "The current best contamination-to-correction pipeline is DCR (EMNLP 2025), which produces a DCR Factor via fuzzy inference across four contamination levels, achieving ~4% average error on three benchmarks — but its ad-hoc multiplicative correction Acc_adj = Acc × (1 − DCR Factor) has no measurement-theoretic justification and empirically weakens on hard tasks (r=0.66). PSN-IRT (AAAI 2026 Oral) demonstrates IRT's power for LLM evaluation using a 4PL model across 12 LLMs on 11 benchmarks (41,871 items), flagging contamination indirectly via anomalous guessing-rate parameters, but produces no contamination-adjusted ability scores; critically, PSN-IRT succeeds with only 12 models by using neural network estimation (pseudo-Siamese architecture) rather than classical MLE, establishing that neural IRT estimation is viable at small model counts. RankLLM (ICLR 2026) provides a strong non-parametric baseline: bidirectional score propagation between models and questions achieves 90% human alignment on 30 models × 35,550 questions, with remarkable stability under model removal (ρ = 0.94 even with 50% pool removed) and 0.006s convergence — but it produces difficulty-weighted rankings without any contamination modeling. RIDE (arXiv 2025) combines IRT with adversarial perturbation for math evaluation — but uses IRT only as a difficulty reward signal for RL-based question rewriting via RIDE-8B, not for joint ability-contamination estimation. JECS (arXiv May 2026) achieves formal conformal guarantees for multi-model decontamination via joint envelope conformal selection, but wastes information by binarizing items into keep/discard rather than producing continuous corrected scores. ConStat (NeurIPS 2024) detects contamination via performance gaps on rephrased samples using a statistical comparison against reference models, but does not model it as a latent variable within a psychometric framework. In psychometrics, the DGM (Shu et al., Psychometrika 2013) uses a gated IRT formulation estimated via hierarchical MCMC to decompose examinee performance into genuine ability and item-preknowledge components — but assumes item exposure status is known a priori, which is unavailable for LLM training data. Two paired-item approaches exist but use no IRT: PaCoST (arXiv 2024) performs paired confidence significance testing for binary contamination detection, and ConStat compares primary vs. reference benchmark performance — both confirm the paired-item signal is informative but neither models it as a latent variable. For adversarial variant generation, MaSTer (arXiv 2026) provides a validated multi-round rewrite-verify pipeline (5 parallel streams × 3 iterations) achieving 45-94% target failure rates on GSM8K and MATH-500 using Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct and SymPy verification; code is claimed at github.com/sustech-nlp/MaSTer but was unavailable as of May 2026 — backup pipelines exist via MathCheck (ICLR 2025, open code) and MATH-Perturb (ICML 2025, 279 expert-crafted perturbations with open code). MathArena (NeurIPS 2025 D&B Track) has expanded to ~900 problems across 2025-2026 competitions (AIME 2026, HMMT Feb 2026, USAMO 2026, ArXivMath monthly, BrokenArxiv, ArXivLean, Visual Math, Project Euler, Apex) with 50+ models, providing rich uncontaminated ground-truth rankings. Recent IRT estimation advances for small samples include Fox (2025, JEBS) demonstrating IRT-BCSM for N=50-100 by analytically integrating out person parameters, and Bayesian hierarchical priors achieving stable 2PL estimation at small sample sizes. Concurrent work search (arXiv, OpenReview, May 2026): no paper attempts joint IRT-based contamination-ability decomposition with paired adversarial items — the three-way intersection remains unoccupied.",
  "inspired_by": "Field guide gaps: 'Contamination-aware IRT' (gap 3), 'Joint contamination-robustness decomposition' (gap 1); Innovation patterns: 'Self-Referential Measurement' (model as own control via original-vs-variant), 'Formal Guarantees on Evaluation Methodology' (identifiability proof for Gated-2PL), 'Detection-to-Correction Bridge' (from detection signals to calibrated ability scores); Key theoretical bridge: DGM (Shu et al. 2013) provides the gated IRT structure for item preknowledge estimated via hierarchical MCMC, which we extend to the LLM contamination setting where item exposure status is unknown but inferred from paired adversarial items; Untried combinations: 'DGM-style gated IRT with adversarial variant generation for LLM evaluation' (primary), 'Conformal p-values as contamination priors for gated IRT' (secondary), 'RankLLM non-parametric ranking as sanity-check baseline for IRT-corrected rankings' (tertiary)",
  "approach": "We extend the Deterministic Gated IRT model (DGM; Shu et al., Psychometrika 2013) from the test-security domain to LLM contamination assessment, introducing the Gated-2PL (G-2PL) model as the primary framework where correct-response probability decomposes into ability-driven and contamination-driven components via a gating mechanism. The key innovation over DGM is that item exposure status is not assumed known but is identified from paired adversarial items.

**Model specification (primary: Gated-2PL):**
- For variant item i*: P(Y_{j,i*}=1 | θ_j) = σ(a_i(θ_j − b_i − δ_i)), a standard 2PL with difficulty shift δ_i
- For original item i: P(Y_{j,i}=1 | θ_j, ξ_j, η_i) = ξ_j·η_i + (1−ξ_j·η_i)·σ(a_i(θ_j − b_i))
- θ_j = model j's genuine reasoning ability (person parameter)
- ξ_j ∈ [0,1] = model j's contamination exposure (person parameter)
- η_i ∈ [0,1] = item i's contamination susceptibility (item parameter)
- a_i, b_i = discrimination and difficulty (shared across original-variant pairs)
- δ_i = variant difficulty shift (estimated from variant calibration)

**Rationale for G-2PL over G-3PL:** The guessing parameter c_i in 3PL requires 200+ examinees for stable estimation under classical methods, while we have only 15-20 models. Dropping c_i to use 2PL eliminates the most problematic parameter for small samples while retaining the core contamination decomposition. PSN-IRT succeeded with 12 models using neural estimation, but their 4PL worked because they had 41,871 items providing massive per-item information; our gated model adds M+K contamination parameters, making parsimony critical. For math benchmarks with open-ended answers (MATH-500, GSM8K), guessing probability is effectively zero, making 2PL substantively appropriate.

**Ablation to Gated-3PL (G-3PL):**
- P(Y_{j,i*}=1 | θ_j) = c_i + (1−c_i)·σ(a_i(θ_j − b_i − δ_i))
- P(Y_{j,i}=1 | θ_j, ξ_j, η_i) = ξ_j·η_i + (1−ξ_j·η_i)·[c_i + (1−c_i)·σ(a_i(θ_j − b_i))]
- c_i fixed to domain-specific constants: c_i = 0 for open-ended math (MATH-500, GSM8K), enabling estimation only for any future MCQ extensions.

**Estimation strategy (fully specified):**
Primary: Bayesian MCMC via NumPyro/Stan with hierarchical priors, following DGM's original estimation framework:
- θ_j ~ N(0, σ²_θ), σ_θ ~ Half-Cauchy(0, 2.5)
- ξ_j ~ Beta(α_ξ, β_ξ), with α_ξ, β_ξ ~ Gamma(2, 1) (hierarchical; allows posterior to concentrate near 0 for clean models or near 1 for heavily contaminated ones)
- η_i ~ Beta(α_η, β_η), with α_η, β_η ~ Gamma(2, 1) (hierarchical)
- a_i ~ LogNormal(0, 0.5) (positive discrimination, weakly informative)
- b_i ~ N(0, 1) (centered difficulty)
- δ_i ~ N(0, 0.5) (variant shifts expected small)
- MCMC: 4 chains × 2,000 warmup + 2,000 samples, NUTS sampler, R̂ < 1.05 convergence criterion
Comparison: Neural estimation extending PSN-IRT's pseudo-Siamese architecture with an additional gating head that outputs (ξ_j, η_i) — trained via binary cross-entropy on the joint original+variant response matrix. This provides a non-Bayesian point estimate comparison.
Ablation: Variational inference via Pyro SVI as a faster alternative to MCMC, using amortized inference for scalability testing.

**Formal identifiability (central theoretical contribution):**
We prove identifiability via a two-step argument: (1) Variant items serve as contamination-free anchors, identifying θ_j and item parameters {a_i, b_i} via standard 2PL identifiability conditions (≥2 items with heterogeneous discriminations; cf. Maris & Bechger 2009). The difficulty shift δ_i is estimated from the variant calibration. (2) Given identified θ_j and item parameters, the original-variant performance gap identifies the bilinear product ξ_j·η_i. Under the rank-1 bilinear decomposition ξ_j·η_i with M models and K items, we have M·K observed gaps constraining M+K−1 free parameters (one fixed for scale), identifiable when M·K > M+K−1, i.e., (M−1)(K−1) > 0. This holds for any M,K ≥ 2. The 2PL formulation avoids the flat-likelihood surfaces that plague 3PL/4PL estimation with few examinees, as the Fisher information matrix for the 2PL is well-conditioned even at M=15.

**Bilinear rank-1 model adequacy plan:**
The rank-1 assumption (ξ_j·η_i) treats contamination as model-global and item-global, which is a first-order approximation — in reality, contamination may be topic-dependent (e.g., a model contaminated on geometry but not algebra). We address this as follows:
(a) Compute standardized residuals r_{j,i} = (Y_{j,i} − P̂_{j,i}) / √(P̂_{j,i}(1−P̂_{j,i})) from the rank-1 fit and report the residual matrix.
(b) Compute Yen's Q3 statistic for local dependence among original items after conditioning on θ_j — systematic topic-structured residuals would indicate rank-1 insufficiency.
(c) Apply person-fit statistics (standardized log-likelihood lz*) to detect models whose original-item response patterns deviate from the G-2PL predictions, flagging potential topic-specific contamination.
(d) If structured residuals emerge, explore rank-2 extension (ξ_j·η_i → ξ_j^(1)·η_i^(1) + ξ_j^(2)·η_i^(2)) or topic-stratified estimation as explicit future work.
(e) Justification for rank-1 as starting point: LLM contamination is primarily driven by overall training data overlap (entire benchmark suites appearing in Common Crawl/web scrapes) rather than topic-selective memorization; the rank-1 model captures this dominant effect.

**Data collection (within 200 H100-hr budget):**
For ~1,000 items from MATH-500 and a GSM8K subset, we generate symbolically-verified adversarial variants. Primary pipeline: MaSTer-style multi-round rewrite-verify using Qwen3.6-27B as rewriter with SymPy answer verification (~25 H100-hrs). Backup (if MaSTer code unavailable by week 1): (a) single-round rewrite-verify pipeline with Qwen3.6-27B + SymPy checking, implementable in 2-3 days; (b) MathCheck (ICLR 2025, open code at github.com/PremiLab-Math/MathCheck) for GSM8K variants; (c) seed with MATH-Perturb's 279 expert-crafted perturbations (ICML 2025, open code at github.com/Kaffaljidhmah2/MATH-Perturb) and extend via LLM rewriting for remaining items. We collect response matrices from 15-20 models: 10 open-weight (DeepSeek-R2 32B, DeepSeek-V4-Flash 284B, Qwen3.6-27B, Qwen3.5-397B-A17B, GLM-5.1 754B-A40B, OLMo-2-13B, Llama-4-Maverick-17B-A400B, Mistral-Large-3, plus 2 smaller reference models) and 5-8 closed-API models (GPT-4o, GPT-5.2, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Gemini 3.1 Pro). For originals, we reuse Open LLM Leaderboard per-item response data (available via HuggingFace API at huggingface.co/datasets/open-llm-leaderboard/results) where available, requiring new inference only for variant items and models not on the leaderboard (~80 H100-hrs for open-weight variant inference, ~60 H100-hrs for missing original runs). IRT fitting is negligible (<1 hr CPU for MCMC).

**Validation (three-pronged, addressing domain mismatch concern):**

(1) External ranking correlation: Kendall-τ of CRADE-corrected ability rankings vs. MathArena 2026 uncontaminated competition rankings (~900 problems, 50+ models), targeting τ ≥ 0.85 (revised from 0.90 given domain mismatch between textbook-style MATH-500/GSM8K and competition-style MathArena). Report bootstrap 95% confidence interval. Compare against: (a) raw accuracy rankings, (b) RankLLM difficulty-weighted rankings, (c) DCR-corrected rankings (r=0.66 on hard tasks), (d) JECS-filtered rankings.

(2) Synthetic contamination injection (causal validation): Deliberately fine-tune OLMo-2-13B on MATH-500 training items (1 epoch, mild contamination following established protocols from contamination survey literature) and re-evaluate. If G-2PL correctly recovers elevated ξ for the fine-tuned model while θ remains stable (matching pre-contamination ability), this provides causal evidence that the decomposition works. Compare fine-tuned ξ against clean OLMo-2-13B ξ via posterior credible interval separation. This is the strongest validation because it provides ground-truth contamination status.

(3) Convergent validity with existing detectors: Correlate G-2PL's per-model ξ_j estimates with: (a) ConStat contamination flags (performance gap on rephrased vs. original), (b) PaCoST binary contamination verdicts (paired confidence significance test), (c) PSN-IRT's anomalous guessing-rate parameters. High concordance validates that ξ captures the same construct; low concordance would require investigation of what ξ uniquely captures beyond existing methods.

(4) Ablation showing differential correction benefit: Demonstrate that CRADE correction improves ranking accuracy (vs. MathArena) more for models with high estimated ξ (provably or detectably contaminated) than for models with low ξ. This confirms the correction is targeted rather than uniformly applied.

**Anchor assumption validation (variant contamination-free):**
(a) Fit standard 2PL to variant-only response matrix and compute item-fit statistics (S-X² or Orlando-Thissen) and person-fit statistics (lz*). Good fit supports the anchor assumption — variants behave like clean IRT items measuring genuine ability.
(b) Check that variant difficulty b_i + δ_i is predictable from original difficulty b_i plus a systematic shift; high-residual outlier items may indicate re-contaminated variants and should be flagged for manual review.
(c) Cross-validation: Hold out 20% of variant items, fit 2PL on remaining 80%, predict held-out responses. Prediction accuracy comparable to full-data fit supports generalizability.
(d) Ablation: Compare CRADE results using MATH-Perturb's expert-crafted perturbations (strongest anchor assumption) vs. MaSTer/LLM-generated variants to assess sensitivity to variant quality.

Ablations: (a) G-2PL vs. G-3PL (with fixed c_i = 0 for math), (b) Bayesian MCMC vs. neural estimation vs. variational inference, (c) number of variant items (100/500/1000), (d) number of models (10/15/20), (e) sensitivity to variant difficulty shift δ_i, (f) rank-1 vs. rank-2 bilinear decomposition if residuals warrant it, (g) RankLLM vs. G-2PL ranking quality.",

## Reviewer feedback (round 3)
Issues: ["MODERATE: No simulation study planned for G-2PL parameter recovery at N=15-20. This is non-negotiable for a psychometric paper. Standard practice requires: (1) generate data from G-2PL with known θ, ξ, η, a, b parameters at N=15 and N=20; (2) fit the model; (3) report bias, RMSE, and 95% credible interval coverage for each parameter type. Without this, reviewers cannot assess whether the model produces meaningful estimates at this unprecedented sample size. Budget: 1-2 days compute on CPU.", "MODERATE: Item-level η_i is practically non-identifiable at N=15-20 — each item's contamination susceptibility is estimated from only 15-20 binary observations, and the bilinear interaction ξ_j·η_i creates scaling indeterminacy. The proposal's model adequacy plan (Q3, lz*, residuals) tests model fit but does not address the fundamental issue that η_i estimates will be dominated by hierarchical priors. The proposal should explicitly acknowledge this limitation, report posterior shrinkage for η_i vs. θ_j, and consider an ablation with person-level-only contamination (dropping η_i, using a simpler ξ_j-only gate).", "MODERATE: No prior sensitivity analysis planned. With N=15-20 per item, posterior estimates for a_i, η_i, and δ_i will be heavily prior-driven. The proposal specifies priors (LogNormal(0,0.5) for a_i, hierarchical Beta for ξ_j/η_i) but does not test sensitivity. Must report results under at least 2-3 meaningfully different prior specifications (e.g., diffuse vs. informative) to demonstrate which conclusions are data-driven vs. prior-driven.", "MINOR: San Martin et al. (Psychometrika 2024) is incorrectly attributed — actual authors are Noventa, Ye, Kelava, and Spoto. San Martin is only cited within that paper.", "MINOR: MaSTer uses LLM-based verification (Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct at 98% precision), not SymPy. The proposal's 'MaSTer-style multi-round rewrite-verify with SymPy verification' is actually a novel hybrid — this should be stated clearly rather than characterized as following MaSTer.", "MINOR: LEGO-IRT (arXiv Oct 2025) is a concurrent IRT-for-LLMs framework (binary+continuous metrics, 70 LLMs, 3% item usage) that should be cited in the landscape analysis, even though it does not address contamination."]
Feedback: The proposal is close to passing — the core idea is verified as novel, theoretically well-grounded, and addressing a real gap. Three additions would push it over the threshold:

(1) **Add simulation study (Week 4, 1-2 days):** Generate 50 synthetic datasets from G-2PL with known parameters at N=15 and N=20. Vary contamination prevalence (10%, 30%, 50% of models contaminated) and contamination strength (weak/moderate/strong ξ). Report: (a) θ_j recovery (bias, RMSE, coverage), (b) ξ_j recovery, (c) η_i recovery, (d) ranking correlation of estimated θ with true θ. This is the single most important addition — without it, the paper will be rejected by any psychometric reviewer.

(2) **Add prior sensitivity analysis:** Report G-2PL results under 3 prior specifications: (a) the proposed hierarchical Beta priors, (b) weakly informative priors (Beta(1,1) for ξ/η, LogNormal(0,1) for a), (c) strongly informative priors based on external contamination detectors (ConStat/PaCoST flags as informative priors on ξ_j). Show which conclusions change and which are robust.

(3) **Explicitly scope item-level vs. person-level claims:** Acknowledge that η_i estimates will have wide posterior intervals and high shrinkage toward hierarchical mean. Frame the primary contribution as person-level decomposition (θ_j, ξ_j rankings) with item-level η_i as secondary/exploratory. Consider an ablation dropping η_i entirely (ξ_j-only gate: P = ξ_j·p_mem + (1-ξ_j)·2PL) — this has only M additional parameters and is far more identifiable.

Also fix: San Martin → Noventa et al. attribution, clarify MaSTer vs. SymPy verification distinction, cite LEGO-IRT.

You are revising a research idea based on reviewer feedback.

**Today's date: 2026-05-28 (UTC).**

## Original idea
{
  "title": "CRADE: Joint Contamination-Ability Decomposition via Gated Item Response Theory with Paired Adversarial Items",
  "core_problem": "No existing framework can determine whether a model fails adversarial benchmark variants because it memorized original answers (contamination) or because it lacks genuine reasoning ability (capability deficit) — all current work observes this entanglement but none models it within a measurement-theoretic framework, preventing trustworthy LLM capability assessment.",
  "opportunity": "Three previously siloed research streams — IRT-based LLM evaluation (PSN-IRT AAAI 2026 Oral, ATLAS, LEGO-IRT), contamination detection/correction (DCR EMNLP 2025, ConStat NeurIPS 2024, JECS arXiv May 2026), and adversarial robustness testing (MaSTer, RIDE, MATH-Perturb ICML 2025) — have each matured independently to the point where their integration is both technically feasible and urgently needed. The critical catalyst is Wang et al.'s ICLR 2026 proof that all likelihood-based contamination detection fails on reasoning models (AUROC ≈ 50%), creating demand for response-pattern-based alternatives that bypass token-probability signals entirely. A key theoretical precedent exists but has never been applied to LLMs: the Deterministic Gated IRT model (DGM; Shu, Henson & Luecht, Psychometrika 2013) decomposes test performance into genuine ability and cheating/preknowledge components conditioned on item exposure status — precisely the structure needed for LLM contamination. PSN-IRT showed IRT works for LLMs (12 models, 41,871 items, 4PL) but left contamination-adjusted scoring as an explicit open question, flagging anomalous guessing-rate parameters as contamination indicators without providing corrected ability estimates. RankLLM (ICLR 2026) demonstrated that non-parametric difficulty-aware ranking achieves 90% human alignment with only a damping hyperparameter — but provides no contamination decomposition, producing rankings without interpretable ability vs. memorization parameters. The AAAI 2027 deadline (abstracts July 21, papers July 28, 2026) is 8 weeks out. Nobody sits at the three-way intersection of IRT estimation, contamination correction, and adversarial pairing because these communities publish at different venues (ACL/EMNLP for contamination, ICLR/NeurIPS for robustness, AAAI for psychometric evaluation, Psychometrika/JEBS for test security).",
  "landscape": "The current best contamination-to-correction pipeline is DCR (EMNLP 2025), which produces a DCR Factor via fuzzy inference across four contamination levels, achieving ~4% average error on three benchmarks — but its ad-hoc multiplicative correction Acc_adj = Acc × (1 − DCR Factor) has no measurement-theoretic justification and empirically weakens on hard tasks (r=0.66). PSN-IRT (AAAI 2026 Oral) demonstrates IRT's power for LLM evaluation using a 4PL model across 12 LLMs on 11 benchmarks (41,871 items), flagging contamination indirectly via anomalous guessing-rate parameters, but produces no contamination-adjusted ability scores; critically, PSN-IRT succeeds with only 12 models by using neural network estimation (pseudo-Siamese architecture) rather than classical MLE, establishing that neural IRT estimation is viable at small model counts. RankLLM (ICLR 2026) provides a strong non-parametric baseline: bidirectional score propagation between models and questions achieves 90% human alignment on 30 models × 35,550 questions, with remarkable stability under model removal (ρ = 0.94 even with 50% pool removed) and 0.006s convergence — but it produces difficulty-weighted rankings without any contamination modeling. RIDE (arXiv 2025) combines IRT with adversarial perturbation for math evaluation — but uses IRT only as a difficulty reward signal for RL-based question rewriting via RIDE-8B, not for joint ability-contamination estimation. JECS (arXiv May 2026) achieves formal conformal guarantees for multi-model decontamination via joint envelope conformal selection, but wastes information by binarizing items into keep/discard rather than producing continuous corrected scores. ConStat (NeurIPS 2024) detects contamination via performance gaps on rephrased samples using a statistical comparison against reference models, but does not model it as a latent variable within a psychometric framework. In psychometrics, the DGM (Shu et al., Psychometrika 2013) uses a gated IRT formulation estimated via hierarchical MCMC to decompose examinee performance into genuine ability and item-preknowledge components — but assumes item exposure status is known a priori, which is unavailable for LLM training data. Two paired-item approaches exist but use no IRT: PaCoST (arXiv 2024) performs paired confidence significance testing for binary contamination detection, and ConStat compares primary vs. reference benchmark performance — both confirm the paired-item signal is informative but neither models it as a latent variable. For adversarial variant generation, MaSTer (arXiv 2026) provides a validated multi-round rewrite-verify pipeline (5 parallel streams × 3 iterations) achieving 45-94% target failure rates on GSM8K and MATH-500 using Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct and SymPy verification; code is claimed at github.com/sustech-nlp/MaSTer but was unavailable as of May 2026 — backup pipelines exist via MathCheck (ICLR 2025, open code) and MATH-Perturb (ICML 2025, 279 expert-crafted perturbations with open code). MathArena (NeurIPS 2025 D&B Track) has expanded to ~900 problems across 2025-2026 competitions (AIME 2026, HMMT Feb 2026, USAMO 2026, ArXivMath monthly, BrokenArxiv, ArXivLean, Visual Math, Project Euler, Apex) with 50+ models, providing rich uncontaminated ground-truth rankings. Recent IRT estimation advances for small samples include Fox (2025, JEBS) demonstrating IRT-BCSM for N=50-100 by analytically integrating out person parameters, and Bayesian hierarchical priors achieving stable 2PL estimation at small sample sizes. Concurrent work search (arXiv, OpenReview, May 2026): no paper attempts joint IRT-based contamination-ability decomposition with paired adversarial items — the three-way intersection remains unoccupied.",
  "inspired_by": "Field guide gaps: 'Contamination-aware IRT' (gap 3), 'Joint contamination-robustness decomposition' (gap 1); Innovation patterns: 'Self-Referential Measurement' (model as own control via original-vs-variant), 'Formal Guarantees on Evaluation Methodology' (identifiability proof for Gated-2PL), 'Detection-to-Correction Bridge' (from detection signals to calibrated ability scores); Key theoretical bridge: DGM (Shu et al. 2013) provides the gated IRT structure for item preknowledge estimated via hierarchical MCMC, which we extend to the LLM contamination setting where item exposure status is unknown but inferred from paired adversarial items; Untried combinations: 'DGM-style gated IRT with adversarial variant generation for LLM evaluation' (primary), 'Conformal p-values as contamination priors for gated IRT' (secondary), 'RankLLM non-parametric ranking as sanity-check baseline for IRT-corrected rankings' (tertiary)",
  "approach": "We extend the Deterministic Gated IRT model (DGM; Shu et al., Psychometrika 2013) from the test-security domain to LLM contamination assessment, introducing the Gated-2PL (G-2PL) model as the primary framework where correct-response probability decomposes into ability-driven and contamination-driven components via a gating mechanism. The key innovation over DGM is that item exposure status is not assumed known but is identified from paired adversarial items.

**Model specification (primary: Gated-2PL):**
- For variant item i*: P(Y_{j,i*}=1 | θ_j) = σ(a_i(θ_j − b_i − δ_i)), a standard 2PL with difficulty shift δ_i
- For original item i: P(Y_{j,i}=1 | θ_j, ξ_j, η_i) = ξ_j·η_i + (1−ξ_j·η_i)·σ(a_i(θ_j − b_i))
- θ_j = model j's genuine reasoning ability (person parameter)
- ξ_j ∈ [0,1] = model j's contamination exposure (person parameter)
- η_i ∈ [0,1] = item i's contamination susceptibility (item parameter)
- a_i, b_i = discrimination and difficulty (shared across original-variant pairs)
- δ_i = variant difficulty shift (estimated from variant calibration)

**Rationale for G-2PL over G-3PL:** The guessing parameter c_i in 3PL requires 200+ examinees for stable estimation under classical methods, while we have only 15-20 models. Dropping c_i to use 2PL eliminates the most problematic parameter for small samples while retaining the core contamination decomposition. PSN-IRT succeeded with 12 models using neural estimation, but their 4PL worked because they had 41,871 items providing massive per-item information; our gated model adds M+K contamination parameters, making parsimony critical. For math benchmarks with open-ended answers (MATH-500, GSM8K), guessing probability is effectively zero, making 2PL substantively appropriate.

**Ablation to Gated-3PL (G-3PL):**
- P(Y_{j,i*}=1 | θ_j) = c_i + (1−c_i)·σ(a_i(θ_j − b_i − δ_i))
- P(Y_{j,i}=1 | θ_j, ξ_j, η_i) = ξ_j·η_i + (1−ξ_j·η_i)·[c_i + (1−c_i)·σ(a_i(θ_j − b_i))]
- c_i fixed to domain-specific constants: c_i = 0 for open-ended math (MATH-500, GSM8K), enabling estimation only for any future MCQ extensions.

**Estimation strategy (fully specified):**
Primary: Bayesian MCMC via NumPyro/Stan with hierarchical priors, following DGM's original estimation framework:
- θ_j ~ N(0, σ²_θ), σ_θ ~ Half-Cauchy(0, 2.5)
- ξ_j ~ Beta(α_ξ, β_ξ), with α_ξ, β_ξ ~ Gamma(2, 1) (hierarchical; allows posterior to concentrate near 0 for clean models or near 1 for heavily contaminated ones)
- η_i ~ Beta(α_η, β_η), with α_η, β_η ~ Gamma(2, 1) (hierarchical)
- a_i ~ LogNormal(0, 0.5) (positive discrimination, weakly informative)
- b_i ~ N(0, 1) (centered difficulty)
- δ_i ~ N(0, 0.5) (variant shifts expected small)
- MCMC: 4 chains × 2,000 warmup + 2,000 samples, NUTS sampler, R̂ < 1.05 convergence criterion
Comparison: Neural estimation extending PSN-IRT's pseudo-Siamese architecture with an additional gating head that outputs (ξ_j, η_i) — trained via binary cross-entropy on the joint original+variant response matrix. This provides a non-Bayesian point estimate comparison.
Ablation: Variational inference via Pyro SVI as a faster alternative to MCMC, using amortized inference for scalability testing.

**Formal identifiability (central theoretical contribution):**
We prove identifiability via a two-step argument: (1) Variant items serve as contamination-free anchors, identifying θ_j and item parameters {a_i, b_i} via standard 2PL identifiability conditions (≥2 items with heterogeneous discriminations; cf. Maris & Bechger 2009). The difficulty shift δ_i is estimated from the variant calibration. (2) Given identified θ_j and item parameters, the original-variant performance gap identifies the bilinear product ξ_j·η_i. Under the rank-1 bilinear decomposition ξ_j·η_i with M models and K items, we have M·K observed gaps constraining M+K−1 free parameters (one fixed for scale), identifiable when M·K > M+K−1, i.e., (M−1)(K−1) > 0. This holds for any M,K ≥ 2. The 2PL formulation avoids the flat-likelihood surfaces that plague 3PL/4PL estimation with few examinees, as the Fisher information matrix for the 2PL is well-conditioned even at M=15.

**Bilinear rank-1 model adequacy plan:**
The rank-1 assumption (ξ_j·η_i) treats contamination as model-global and item-global, which is a first-order approximation — in reality, contamination may be topic-dependent (e.g., a model contaminated on geometry but not algebra). We address this as follows:
(a) Compute standardized residuals r_{j,i} = (Y_{j,i} − P̂_{j,i}) / √(P̂_{j,i}(1−P̂_{j,i})) from the rank-1 fit and report the residual matrix.
(b) Compute Yen's Q3 statistic for local dependence among original items after conditioning on θ_j — systematic topic-structured residuals would indicate rank-1 insufficiency.
(c) Apply person-fit statistics (standardized log-likelihood lz*) to detect models whose original-item response patterns deviate from the G-2PL predictions, flagging potential topic-specific contamination.
(d) If structured residuals emerge, explore rank-2 extension (ξ_j·η_i → ξ_j^(1)·η_i^(1) + ξ_j^(2)·η_i^(2)) or topic-stratified estimation as explicit future work.
(e) Justification for rank-1 as starting point: LLM contamination is primarily driven by overall training data overlap (entire benchmark suites appearing in Common Crawl/web scrapes) rather than topic-selective memorization; the rank-1 model captures this dominant effect.

**Data collection (within 200 H100-hr budget):**
For ~1,000 items from MATH-500 and a GSM8K subset, we generate symbolically-verified adversarial variants. Primary pipeline: MaSTer-style multi-round rewrite-verify using Qwen3.6-27B as rewriter with SymPy answer verification (~25 H100-hrs). Backup (if MaSTer code unavailable by week 1): (a) single-round rewrite-verify pipeline with Qwen3.6-27B + SymPy checking, implementable in 2-3 days; (b) MathCheck (ICLR 2025, open code at github.com/PremiLab-Math/MathCheck) for GSM8K variants; (c) seed with MATH-Perturb's 279 expert-crafted perturbations (ICML 2025, open code at github.com/Kaffaljidhmah2/MATH-Perturb) and extend via LLM rewriting for remaining items. We collect response matrices from 15-20 models: 10 open-weight (DeepSeek-R2 32B, DeepSeek-V4-Flash 284B, Qwen3.6-27B, Qwen3.5-397B-A17B, GLM-5.1 754B-A40B, OLMo-2-13B, Llama-4-Maverick-17B-A400B, Mistral-Large-3, plus 2 smaller reference models) and 5-8 closed-API models (GPT-4o, GPT-5.2, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Gemini 3.1 Pro). For originals, we reuse Open LLM Leaderboard per-item response data (available via HuggingFace API at huggingface.co/datasets/open-llm-leaderboard/results) where available, requiring new inference only for variant items and models not on the leaderboard (~80 H100-hrs for open-weight variant inference, ~60 H100-hrs for missing original runs). IRT fitting is negligible (<1 hr CPU for MCMC).

**Validation (three-pronged, addressing domain mismatch concern):**

(1) External ranking correlation: Kendall-τ of CRADE-corrected ability rankings vs. MathArena 2026 uncontaminated competition rankings (~900 problems, 50+ models), targeting τ ≥ 0.85 (revised from 0.90 given domain mismatch between textbook-style MATH-500/GSM8K and competition-style MathArena). Report bootstrap 95% confidence interval. Compare against: (a) raw accuracy rankings, (b) RankLLM difficulty-weighted rankings, (c) DCR-corrected rankings (r=0.66 on hard tasks), (d) JECS-filtered rankings.

(2) Synthetic contamination injection (causal validation): Deliberately fine-tune OLMo-2-13B on MATH-500 training items (1 epoch, mild contamination following established protocols from contamination survey literature) and re-evaluate. If G-2PL correctly recovers elevated ξ for the fine-tuned model while θ remains stable (matching pre-contamination ability), this provides causal evidence that the decomposition works. Compare fine-tuned ξ against clean OLMo-2-13B ξ via posterior credible interval separation. This is the strongest validation because it provides ground-truth contamination status.

(3) Convergent validity with existing detectors: Correlate G-2PL's per-model ξ_j estimates with: (a) ConStat contamination flags (performance gap on rephrased vs. original), (b) PaCoST binary contamination verdicts (paired confidence significance test), (c) PSN-IRT's anomalous guessing-rate parameters. High concordance validates that ξ captures the same construct; low concordance would require investigation of what ξ uniquely captures beyond existing methods.

(4) Ablation showing differential correction benefit: Demonstrate that CRADE correction improves ranking accuracy (vs. MathArena) more for models with high estimated ξ (provably or detectably contaminated) than for models with low ξ. This confirms the correction is targeted rather than uniformly applied.

**Anchor assumption validation (variant contamination-free):**
(a) Fit standard 2PL to variant-only response matrix and compute item-fit statistics (S-X² or Orlando-Thissen) and person-fit statistics (lz*). Good fit supports the anchor assumption — variants behave like clean IRT items measuring genuine ability.
(b) Check that variant difficulty b_i + δ_i is predictable from original difficulty b_i plus a systematic shift; high-residual outlier items may indicate re-contaminated variants and should be flagged for manual review.
(c) Cross-validation: Hold out 20% of variant items, fit 2PL on remaining 80%, predict held-out responses. Prediction accuracy comparable to full-data fit supports generalizability.
(d) Ablation: Compare CRADE results using MATH-Perturb's expert-crafted perturbations (strongest anchor assumption) vs. MaSTer/LLM-generated variants to assess sensitivity to variant quality.

Ablations: (a) G-2PL vs. G-3PL (with fixed c_i = 0 for math), (b) Bayesian MCMC vs. neural estimation vs. variational inference, (c) number of variant items (100/500/1000), (d) number of models (10/15/20), (e) sensitivity to variant difficulty shift δ_i, (f) rank-1 vs. rank-2 bilinear decomposition if residuals warrant it, (g) RankLLM vs. G-2PL ranking quality.",

Issues: ["MODERATE: No simulation study planned for G-2PL parameter recovery at N=15-20. This is non-negotiable for a psychometric paper. The proposal's model adequacy plan (Q3, lz*, residuals) tests model fit but does not address the fundamental issue that η_i estimates will be dominated by hierarchical priors. With N=15-20 per item, posterior estimates for a_i, η_i, and δ_i will be heavily prior-driven. The proposal specifies priors (LogNormal(0,0.5) for a_i, hierarchical Beta for ξ_j/η_i) but does not test sensitivity. (Psychometrika 2024) is incorrectly attributed — actual authors are Noventa, Ye, Kelava, and Spoto. San Martin is only cited within that paper.", "MINOR: MaSTer uses LLM-based verification (Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct at 98% precision), not SymPy. The proposal's 'MaSTer-style multi-round rewrite-verify with SymPy verification' is actually a novel hybrid — this should be stated clearly rather than characterized as following MaSTer.", "MINOR: LEGO-IRT (arXiv Oct 2025) is a concurrent IRT-for-LLMs framework (binary+continuous metrics, 70 LLMs, 3% item usage) that should be cited in the landscape analysis, even though it does not address contamination."]
Feedback: The proposal is close to passing — the core idea is verified as novel, theoretically well-grounded, and addressing a real gap. Three additions would push it over the threshold:

(1) **Add simulation study (Week 4, 1-2 days):** Generate 50 synthetic datasets from G-2PL with known parameters at N=15 and N=20. Vary contamination prevalence (10%, 30%, 50% of models contaminated) and contamination strength (weak/moderate/strong ξ). Report: (a) θ_j recovery (bias, RMSE, coverage), (b) ξ_j recovery, (c) η_i recovery, (d) ranking correlation of estimated θ with true θ. This is the single most important addition — without it, the paper will be rejected by any psychometric reviewer.

(2) **Add prior sensitivity analysis:** Report G-2PL results under 3 prior specifications: (a) the proposed hierarchical Beta priors, (b) weakly informative priors (Beta(1,1) for ξ/η, LogNormal(0,1) for a), (c) strongly informative priors based on external contamination detectors (ConStat/PaCoST flags as informative priors on ξ_j). Show which conclusions change and which are robust.

(3) **Explicitly scope item-level vs. person-level claims:** Acknowledge that η_i estimates will have wide posterior intervals and high shrinkage toward hierarchical mean. Frame the primary contribution as person-level decomposition (θ_j, ξ_j rankings) with item-level η_i as secondary/exploratory. Consider an ablation dropping η_i entirely (ξ_j-only gate: P = ξ_j·p_mem + (1-ξ_j)·2PL) — this has only M additional parameters and is far more identifiable.

Also fix: San Martin → Noventa et al. attribution, clarify MaSTer vs. SymPy verification distinction, cite LEGO-IRT.

## Instructions
- Think in two phases: FIRST reconsider the problem framing (core_problem / opportunity / landscape) if the reviewer flagged issues there, THEN revise the method.
- Address each issue specifically.

## 深度调研要求

不要简单地'打补丁'——每一轮修订都是重新审视和深化的机会。

1. **深度搜索**：针对 reviewer 指出的每个问题，用 2-3 种不同的搜索查询调研。
2. **深度阅读**：用 WebFetch 实际阅读找到的关键论文。
3. **深度思考**：
   - 核心假设是否仍然成立？
   - reviewer 的批评是否揭示了更深层的问题？
   - 有没有更好的 framing 或 approach？
4. **避免表面修订**：如果反复 minor fix 没有实质改进，考虑 major revision 或 pivot。

## 针对 Review 意见的定向搜索

1. **如果'已有类似工作'**：搜索并阅读相关论文，明确差异化点
2. **如果'SOTA 过时'**：查看 Papers With Code 排行榜，更新 baseline
3. **如果'可行性有问题'**：搜索类似实验成本和 GitHub 实现
4. **如果'novelty 不足'**：做 3-5 种关键词搜索，考虑 major revision 或 pivot

- You have full freedom: minor fix, major revision, or pivot.
- Include a "change_type" field: "minor", "major", or "pivot".
- Output a COMPLETE JSON object with ALL fields.

2. What does the literature say about IRT parameter recovery at very small N (N<30)?

3. Search for "simulation study IRT parameter recovery" on arXiv and Google Scholar

4. Search for any papers doing simulation studies with bilinear or multiplicative IRT parameters (like our ξ_j·η_i interaction term)

Use WebSearch and WebFetch to find and read relevant papers. Report specific findings about:
- Minimum viable N for 2PL recovery
- Whether bilinear interaction parameters can be recovered at N=15-20
- Best practices for reporting simulation results
- Any papers that do IRT with <30 examinees

Keep your report under 500 words, focused on actionable findings.

input.prompt:
I'm researching two related issues for a Bayesian IRT paper:

## Issue 1: Prior sensitivity analysis in Bayesian IRT
I'm using a Gated 2PL IRT model with only N=15-20 examinees. Priors are:
- θ_j ~ N(0, σ²_θ), σ_θ ~ Half-Cauchy(0, 2.5)
- ξ_j ~ Beta(α_ξ, β_ξ), hierarchical
- η_i ~ Beta(α_η, β_η), hierarchical  
- a_i ~ LogNormal(0, 0.5)
- b_i ~ N(0, 1)

A reviewer demands prior sensitivity analysis under at least 2-3 prior specifications. Search for:
1. "Prior sensitivity analysis Bayesian IRT" - what's standard practice?
2. "Weakly informative priors IRT" - what are common choices?
3. Papers that demonstrate prior sensitivity for IRT at small sample sizes
4. How is prior sensitivity typically reported? (tables of parameter estimates under different priors, Bayes factor comparisons, etc.)

## Issue 2: Identifiability of item-level parameters in bilinear models at small N
My model has a bilinear interaction ξ_j·η_i where:
- ξ_j = per-model contamination (15-20 values)
- η_i = per-item contamination susceptibility (~1000 values)
- Each η_i is estimated from only 15-20 binary observations

The reviewer says η_i will be "dominated by hierarchical priors" and suggests a simpler ξ_j-only model as an ablation. Search for:
1. "Bilinear model identifiability small sample" 
2. "Posterior shrinkage hierarchical Bayesian" - how is shrinkage quantified?
3. "Item parameter recovery small sample IRT" - what happens to item parameters at N<30?
4. Any literature on person-only vs. person×item interaction models in cheating detection

Also search for: "simplified cheating detection model IRT" or "person-level cheating parameter IRT" to see if ξ_j-only models exist in the psychometric cheating detection literature.

Use WebSearch and WebFetch. Report actionable findings under 500 words.

Based on the search results, here are key findings about IRT parameter recovery with small sample sizes using Bayesian approaches:

## Bayesian Methods for Small Samples

Long-standing difficulties in estimating item parameters in item response theory (IRT) have been addressed recently with the application of Bayesian estimation models. Parameters can be recovered fairly well using WinBUGS with Bayesian estimation.

## Recommended Sample Sizes and Priors

The two-parameter logistic (2PL) model has a recommended sample size of N ≥ 500; however, smaller sample sizes are possible when prior information is available. Bayesian priors are often applied when estimating 3PL models, especially with small samples.

Importantly, for samples of 100, priors on both the a-parameters and c-parameters were needed to avoid estimation problems, suggesting that prior specification becomes increasingly critical as sample sizes decrease below N=100.

## Hierarchical Bayesian Approach

Using Markov chain Monte Carlo in a hierarchical Bayesian framework, the item parameters, the overall and domain-specific abilities, and their correlations are estimated simultaneously. A larger sample size resulted in a better estimate of the model parameters, and a longer test length yielded better individual ability recovery.

## Convergence Issues

An extremely small sample size (e.g., N = 25 or 50) might result in model non-convergence issues.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about IRT simulation study best practices regarding parameter recovery, replications, and metrics:

## Parameter Recovery Studies

Parameter recovery studies evaluate how well IRT parameters can be estimated by generating datasets with known parameters using Monte Carlo simulation methods, then calibrating the data under different conditions and comparing recovered parameters to the original known parameters. If calibrated parameters are quite similar to the original parameters, the calibration can be interpreted as accurate.

## Number of Replications

Studies vary considerably in their replication counts. The search results show examples ranging from 20 replications to 2000 replicates depending on the study design. A recommended approach is to conduct a pilot study where the simulation procedure is implemented on selected conditions for a large number of replications, and mean values of the dependent variables are examined as a function of the number of replications to determine an appropriate number.

## Assessment Metrics

For evaluating parameter recovery, comparisons are made between estimated parameters and known parameters based on standardized bias, and root mean square error (RMSE) is calculated to provide a standard deviation of the residuals. Additionally, while previous research has primarily evaluated the absolute deviation of estimated parameters from true parameters, in diagnostic contexts the correlation between these values is often more relevant for ensuring validity.

## Simulation Design Factors

Common factors varied in simulation designs include sample size, test length, and scale correlations in a completely crossed design.

**Publication:** The IRT-BCSM is a latent-variable-free model and consists of (fixed) item parameters and a common covariance parameter, where person parameters can be post-hoc sampled.

**Main Contribution:** The two-parameter IRT model is redefined by analytically integrating out the random person factor in the latent response formulation of the model to make it suitable for small sample applications.

**The IRT-BCSM Model:** This IRT Bayesian covariance structure model (IRT-BCSM) describes the clustering of (latent) responses by persons through a structured covariance matrix in which a common covariance parameter represents the dependence implied by a unidimensional random factor variable.

**Estimation Method:** An efficient Gibbs sampler is proposed for parameter estimation.

**Performance in Small Samples:** In simulation studies, the performance of the IRT-BCSM is compared to two-parameter IRT models for small samples, and results show an optimal performance of the IRT-BCSM even in sample sizes as small as 50 to 100 persons and 5 to 10 items.

Based on the search results, here are key findings about IRT parameter recovery with small sample sizes using Bayesian approaches:

## Bayesian Methods for Small Samples

Long-standing difficulties in estimating item parameters in item response theory (IRT) have been addressed recently with the application of Bayesian estimation models. Parameters can be recovered fairly well using WinBUGS with Bayesian estimation.

## Recommended Sample Sizes and Priors

The two-parameter logistic (2PL) model has a recommended sample size of N ≥ 500; however, smaller sample sizes are possible when prior information is available. Bayesian priors are often applied when estimating 3PL models, especially with small samples.

Importantly, for samples of 100, priors on both the a-parameters and c-parameters were needed to avoid estimation problems, suggesting that prior specification becomes increasingly critical as sample sizes decrease below N=100.

## Hierarchical Bayesian Approach

Using Markov chain Monte Carlo in a hierarchical Bayesian framework, the item parameters, the overall and domain-specific abilities, and their correlations are estimated simultaneously. A larger sample size resulted in a better estimate of the model parameters, and a longer test length yielded better individual ability recovery.

## Convergence Issues

An extremely small sample size (e.g., N = 25 or 50) might result in model non-convergence issues.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about IRT simulation study best practices regarding parameter recovery, replications, and metrics:

## Parameter Recovery Studies

Parameter recovery studies evaluate how well IRT parameters can be estimated by generating datasets with known parameters using Monte Carlo simulation methods, then calibrating the data under different conditions and comparing recovered parameters to the original known parameters. If calibrated parameters are quite similar to the original parameters, the calibration can be interpreted as accurate.

## Number of Replications

Studies vary considerably in their replication counts. The search results show examples ranging from 20 replications to 2000 replicates depending on the study design. A recommended approach is to conduct a pilot study where the simulation procedure is implemented on selected conditions for a large number of replications, and mean values of the dependent variables are examined as a function of the number of replications to determine an appropriate number.

## Assessment Metrics

For evaluating parameter recovery, comparisons are made between estimated parameters and known parameters based on standardized bias, and root mean square error (RMSE) is calculated to provide a standard deviation of the residuals. Additionally, while previous research has primarily evaluated the absolute deviation of estimated parameters from true parameters, in diagnostic contexts the correlation between these values is often more relevant for ensuring validity.

## Simulation Design Factors

Common factors varied in simulation designs include sample size, test length, and scale correlations in a completely crossed design.

## Key Studies and Findings:

**2PL Testlet Model Study:**
A comprehensive simulation study was conducted to investigate how MCMC, MMLE, and limited information estimation methods recovered the item parameters of the 2PL testlet model, with manipulated factors including sample size and testlet effect magnitude. The study found no statistically significant differences regarding parameter recovery between the three methods.

**Multidimensional 2PL (M2PL) Parameter Recovery:**
Simulation analyses evaluated parameter recovery for the multidimensional two-parameter logistic model (M2PL) under varying conditions of sample size (1,000, 3,000), number of items (25, 50), and correlation between abilities (.0, .3, and .6).

**IRTree Models with 2PL:**
A Monte Carlo simulation study explored the ability of IRTree models to recover item parameters, with results indicating the IRTree model can adequately recover item parameters early in the decision process model, specifically the midpoint node, but as the model progresses through the decision hierarchy, item parameters have increased associated error variance.

These studies demonstrate that Monte Carlo simulation approaches are commonly used to evaluate parameter recovery performance across different estimation methods and model conditions in IRT research with 2PL models.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about posterior shrinkage in hierarchical Bayesian models:

## Key Concepts

**Hierarchical Shrinkage**: Hierarchical Bayesian inference can be used to estimate unknown prior parameters from the data, by allowing the prior variances of regression coefficients to have a hyperprior distribution. Bayes shrinkage estimators for dynamic regressions are based on hierarchical versions of the typical normal prior, and various popular penalized least squares estimators for shrinkage and selection in regression models can be recovered using a single hierarchical Bayes formulation.

**Posterior Shrinkage in Practice**: In hierarchical models, there can be dramatic shrinkage of estimates toward the average, with the amount of shrinkage depending on the amount of individual data available.

**Quantifying Uncertainty**: There's an important distinction to make: Bayesian analogs of convex penalties (such as Laplace priors for Bayesian Lasso) lead to sub-optimal uncertainty quantification. This is relevant when reporting posterior inference, as proper uncertainty quantification is critical.

**Advanced Applications**: Two-step procedures combine shrinkage through continuous priors with sparsification, and can be used to communicate to policymakers which variables drive specific outcomes.

The search results show that hierarchical Bayesian shrinkage is widely used in regression analysis, quantile regression, and high-dimensional problems, with careful attention needed to proper uncertainty quantification when reporting results.

## Issue 1: Prior Sensitivity Analysis

**Standard practice** (per [van Erp et al., 2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7721677/)): Run 2-3 alternative prior specifications alongside your reference priors and compare posterior estimates, credible intervals, and convergence diagnostics. The recommended workflow is: (1) fit with original priors, (2) specify alternatives without peeking at results, (3) refit and compare, (4) report side-by-side.

**What to vary for your model:**
- For `a_i ~ LogNormal(0, 0.5)`: test LogNormal(0, 0.25) (tighter) and LogNormal(0, 1.0) (vaguer). The [PMC item parameter recovery study](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11268390/) shows discrimination priors tolerate moderate variation but are sensitive to extreme informativeness.
- For `b_i ~ N(0, 1)`: test N(0, 1.5) and N(0, 0.5).
- For `sigma_theta ~ Half-Cauchy(0, 2.5)`: test Half-Cauchy(0, 1) and Half-Cauchy(0, 5). The [OH2PL study](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10700496/) found Half-Cauchy and Exponential hyperpriors outperformed inverse-Gamma, producing unbiased estimates even at N=50.

**How to report:** Present a table of posterior means, SDs, and 95% HDIs under each specification. Overlay posterior density plots for key parameters. Report percent deviation from the reference specification. At N=15-20, expect visible sensitivity; the goal is showing conclusions are qualitatively stable, not numerically identical.

## Issue 2: Bilinear Identifiability and the Ablation

**The reviewer is correct that eta_i will be heavily shrunk.** With 15-20 binary observations per item, individual eta_i estimates will be dominated by the hierarchical prior. [Konig & Alexandrowicz (2024)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10846471/) show that in hierarchical Bayesian IRT, individual parameters shrink toward the grand mean as effective sample size decreases. With only 15-20 observations per eta_i, these are essentially unidentifiable individually ("pre-asymptotically non-identifiable").

**How to quantify shrinkage:** Compare each eta_i posterior to the hierarchical prior. If the posterior SD is barely narrower than the prior SD, the data contribute almost no information. Report the ratio `prior_SD / posterior_SD` -- values near 1.0 confirm prior dominance. Also report the effective shrinkage: `(eta_i_posterior_mean - prior_mean) / (eta_i_MLE - prior_mean)` where values near 0 mean total shrinkage to the prior.

**The ablation is well-motivated.** The DGM literature (Shu, Leucht, & Henson, 2013; discussed on [Stan Forums](https://discourse.mc-stan.org/t/syntax-for-irt-model-for-detecting-cheating/4152)) uses person-level cheating parameters with item status treated as known or estimated separately -- effectively a xi_j-only model. A simplified model dropping eta_i (replacing xi_j * eta_i with just xi_j) is defensible as a standard approach in the cheating detection literature. Run both models, compare via LOO-CV or WAIC, and report whether the interaction term improves out-of-sample prediction. If it does not meaningfully improve fit, the simpler model is preferable. If it does, the hierarchical eta_i still has value as a population-level summary even if individual estimates are shrunk.

**Key recommendation:** Frame eta_i not as individually identified parameters but as contributing to a better-estimated population-level hyperparameter (the distribution of item susceptibility), which regularizes xi_j estimates.

**IRT Simulation Study Research Findings for Gated 2PL with N=15-20**

**1. Standard Practices for IRT Simulation Studies**

- **Replications:** 100 is the most common baseline (used by Konig et al., HBMIRT paper, and the Bulut simulation textbook). Some studies use 50 (for computationally expensive MCMC), others 1000+ for simple models. The IRTree study used 2000. The practical recommendation: start with 100; verify stability by running a subset at 150. For Bayesian MCMC models, 50-100 replications is defensible if each replication is expensive.
- **Metrics:** The standard set is **bias**, **RMSE**, and **correlation** between true and estimated parameters. Many studies also report **coverage rates** of 95% credible intervals and **interval length**. Convergence rate is critical for small-N conditions.
- **Factors varied:** Sample size (N), test length (number of items), and parameter distributions (discrimination/difficulty ranges). A fully crossed design is standard.

**2. Minimum Viable N for 2PL Recovery**

The literature floor is **N=50**, not lower. Key evidence:
- Konig et al. (2020/2023) tested N=50, 75, 100, 150, 200, 500 with an optimized hierarchical Bayesian 2PL. At N=50, MML had 75-89% inadmissible solutions; hierarchical Bayes succeeded but with elevated RMSE.
- HBMIRT (2024) tested N=50, 100, 500. Hierarchical priors produced minimal bias at N=50 (bias=0.050 for slopes vs. 0.215 for ML). All Bayesian runs converged at N=50.
- Fox (2025, JEBS) IRT-BCSM integrates out person parameters and works at N=50-100, but was **not tested below N=50**.
- de la Torre & Hong (2010) used hierarchical Bayesian higher-order IRT for small samples but studied item calibration, not examinee counts as low as 15-20.
- **No published study was found that recovers standard 2PL parameters at N<50.** At N=25, convergence failures are documented as frequent.

**3. Bilinear/Multiplicative Interaction Parameters**

No simulation study was found specifically addressing parameter recovery for bilinear/multiplicative interaction terms (like your gating parameter product) in an IRT framework. This is a gap. The identifiability literature on multiplicative latent factor models warns that such terms face severe identifiability challenges with few observations, compounded at small N. You would be contributing novel methodology here, which strengthens the case for a simulation study but also means there is no established benchmark to cite.

**4. IRT with LLMs as Examinees (<30)**

IRT-Router used 20 LLMs but performed no parameter recovery study and did not acknowledge the small-N issue. Most IRT-for-LLM papers (tinyBenchmarks, Latency-Response Theory) treat items as the estimation target and LLMs as fixed, sidestepping person-parameter recovery. No paper was found doing rigorous IRT parameter recovery validation at N=15-20 examinees.

**5. Actionable Recommendations**

- Run **100 replications** minimum (50 acceptable if computation is prohibitive; justify with stability analysis).
- Report **bias, RMSE, correlation, and 95% credible interval coverage** for all parameters (discrimination, difficulty, gating, ability).

- For the bilinear gating term, consider a **profile of recovery** showing how correlation between true and estimated values degrades as N shrinks from 100 to 15.

The key innovation over DGM is that item exposure status is not assumed known but is identified from paired adversarial items.

**Model hierarchy (from simple to complex):**

**Model 1 — Person-Gated 2PL (PG-2PL, primary model):**
- For variant item i*: P(Y_{j,i*}=1 | θ_j) = σ(a_i(θ_j − b_i − δ_i))
- For original item i: P(Y_{j,i}=1 | θ_j, ξ_j) = ξ_j·p_{mem,i} + (1−ξ_j)·σ(a_i(θ_j − b_i))
- θ_j = model j's genuine reasoning ability (person parameter)
- ξ_j ∈ [0,1] = model j's contamination exposure (person parameter)
- p_{mem,i} = probability of correct answer given memorization, fixed to empirical ceiling (e.g., 0.95 for exact-match items, 1.0 for items with unique answers)
- a_i, b_i = discrimination and difficulty (shared across original-variant pairs)
- δ_i = variant difficulty shift
- This model adds only M contamination parameters (one per model), each estimated from ~K=1000 original-variant performance gaps — robustly identifiable even at M=15.

**Rationale for PG-2PL as primary:** At N=15-20 models, each item-level parameter is estimated from only 15-20 binary observations. The IRT small-sample literature establishes that even standard 2PL item parameter recovery is marginal at N=50 (Fox 2025 JEBS; OH2PL studies) and prone to convergence failures at N=25 (Sehgal et al. 2023). Adding per-item contamination susceptibility η_i in the bilinear model would yield estimates dominated by hierarchical prior shrinkage, providing little item-level information beyond the prior mean. The PG-2PL avoids this: it treats contamination as a model-level property (how contaminated is this LLM overall?) rather than attempting to distinguish which specific items each model memorized — a more appropriate level of resolution given the person-rich, model-poor data structure.

**Model 2 — Bilinear-Gated 2PL (BG-2PL, extended model):**
- For original item i: P(Y_{j,i}=1 | θ_j, ξ_j, η_i) = ξ_j·η_i + (1−ξ_j·η_i)·σ(a_i(θ_j − b_i))
- η_i ∈ [0,1] = item i's contamination susceptibility (item parameter)
- Adds K item-level contamination parameters, each estimated from only M=15-20 observations
- Presented as an extension with explicit acknowledgment that η_i estimates will exhibit high posterior shrinkage toward the hierarchical mean and wide credible intervals
- Model comparison via WAIC/LOO-CV between PG-2PL and BG-2PL determines whether the data supports item-level contamination resolution

**Model 0 — Standard 2PL baseline:**
- Fit standard 2PL on variant-only response matrix
- Provides contamination-free θ_j estimates as ground truth for validating Models 1 and 2

**Rationale for 2PL over 3PL:** The guessing parameter c_i in 3PL requires 200+ examinees for stable estimation under classical methods, while we have only 15-20 models. For math benchmarks with open-ended answers (MATH-500, GSM8K), guessing probability is effectively zero, making 2PL substantively appropriate. PSN-IRT succeeded with 4PL because they had 41,871 items providing massive per-item information; our gated model adds contamination parameters, making parsimony critical.

**Estimation strategy (fully specified):**
Primary: Bayesian MCMC via NumPyro/Stan with hierarchical priors:
- θ_j ~ N(0, σ²_θ), σ_θ ~ Half-Cauchy(0, 2.5)
- ξ_j ~ Beta(α_ξ, β_ξ), with α_ξ, β_ξ ~ Gamma(2, 1) (hierarchical)
- For BG-2PL: η_i ~ Beta(α_η, β_η), with α_η, β_η ~ Gamma(2, 1) (hierarchical)
- a_i ~ LogNormal(0, 0.5) (positive discrimination, weakly informative)
- b_i ~ N(0, 1) (centered difficulty)
- δ_i ~ N(0, 0.5) (variant shifts expected small)
- MCMC: 4 chains × 2,000 warmup + 2,000 samples, NUTS sampler, R̂ < 1.05 convergence criterion
Comparison: Neural estimation extending PSN-IRT's pseudo-Siamese architecture with an additional gating head that outputs ξ_j (and optionally η_i) — trained via binary cross-entropy on the joint original+variant response matrix.
Ablation: Variational inference via Pyro SVI as a faster alternative to MCMC.

**Simulation study for parameter recovery (central methodological contribution):**
This is the single most critical experiment — without it, no psychometric reviewer will accept the paper. Design:
- Generate 100 synthetic datasets from each model (PG-2PL, BG-2PL) with known ground-truth parameters at M=15 and M=20 models, K=500 and K=1000 items.
- Vary contamination prevalence: 10%, 30%, 50% of models have ξ_j > 0.3 (contaminated)
- Vary contamination strength: weak (ξ_j ~ Beta(2,8), mean 0.2), moderate (ξ_j ~ Beta(5,5), mean 0.5), strong (ξ_j ~ Beta(8,2), mean 0.8)
- For BG-2PL: vary η_i heterogeneity (low: η_i ~ Beta(10,2) concentrated near 0.83; high: η_i ~ Beta(2,2) spread across [0,1])
- Report per parameter type: (a) bias = E[θ̂_j − θ_j], (b) RMSE = √E[(θ̂_j − θ_j)²], (c) 95% credible interval coverage, (d) Kendall-τ of estimated vs. true ranking
- Key hypothesis: θ_j and ξ_j recovery will be good (each informed by K≈1000 items) while η_i recovery will be poor (each informed by only M=15-20 models), confirming the PG-2PL as the appropriate primary model
- Separately report posterior shrinkage for η_i: compute ratio of posterior SD to prior SD, and correlation between posterior means and true values — high shrinkage ratio with low correlation confirms that η_i estimates are prior-dominated

**Formal identifiability:**
Model 1 (PG-2PL): (1) Variant items serve as contamination-free anchors, identifying θ_j and item parameters {a_i, b_i} via standard 2PL identifiability conditions (≥2 items with heterogeneous discriminations; cf. Maris & Bechger 2009). (2) Given identified θ_j and item parameters, the original-item performance gap ΔP_{j,i} = P_obs(Y_{j,i}=1) − σ(a_i(θ_j − b_i)) identifies ξ_j from K original items via moment matching. With K=1000 items, the law of large numbers ensures ξ̂_j is consistent. (3) PG-2PL has M+K standard IRT parameters + M contamination parameters = 2M+K total parameters, estimated from M×2K binary observations. The ratio of observations to parameters is 2MK/(2M+K), which is ~1970/1020 ≈ 1.93 at M=15, K=500 — tight but feasible with Bayesian regularization; at K=1000 it is ~30000/1030 ≈ 29.1, well-identified.

Model 2 (BG-2PL): Extends PG-2PL with K additional η_i parameters. The bilinear product ξ_j·η_i has M·K observed gaps constraining M+K−1 free parameters. Identifiable when (M−1)(K−1) > 0 (any M,K ≥ 2). However, practical identifiability at M=15-20 is limited: η_i posterior intervals will be wide, and the model is treated as exploratory.

**Bilinear rank-1 model adequacy plan (for BG-2PL):**
(a) Compute standardized residuals r_{j,i} from the PG-2PL fit — systematic item-structured patterns indicate need for item-level η_i.
(b) Compute Yen's Q3 statistic for local dependence among original items after conditioning on θ_j.
(c) Apply person-fit statistics (lz*) to detect models whose response patterns deviate from PG-2PL predictions.
(d) Compare WAIC/LOO-CV between PG-2PL and BG-2PL to formally test whether item-level contamination parameters improve predictive accuracy beyond shrinkage-dominated noise.
(e) Report posterior shrinkage ratio for η_i estimates: Var(η_i|data)/Var(η_i|prior). Values close to 1.0 indicate the data provides no information beyond the prior; values < 0.5 indicate meaningful item-level signal.

For ~1,000 items from MATH-500 and a GSM8K subset, we generate adversarial variants with verified answers. ## Issue 1: Prior Sensitivity Analysis

**Standard practice** (per [van Erp et al., 2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7721677/)): Run 2-3 alternative prior specifications alongside your reference priors and compare posterior estimates, credible intervals, and convergence diagnostics. The recommended workflow is: (1) fit with original priors, (2) specify alternatives without peeking at results, (3) refit and compare, (4) report side-by-side.

**What to vary for your model:**
- For `a_i ~ LogNormal(0, 0.5)`: test LogNormal(0, 0.25) (tighter) and LogNormal(0, 1.0) (vaguer). The [PMC item parameter recovery study](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11268390/) shows discrimination priors tolerate moderate variation but are sensitive to extreme informativeness.
- For `b_i ~ N(0, 1)`: test N(0, 1.5) and N(0, 0.5).
- For `sigma_theta ~ Half-Cauchy(0, 2.5)`: test Half-Cauchy(0, 1) and Half-Cauchy(0, 5). The [OH2PL study](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10700496/) found Half-Cauchy and Exponential hyperpriors outperformed inverse-Gamma, producing unbiased estimates even at N=50.

**How to report:** Present a table of posterior means, SDs, and 95% HDIs under each specification. Overlay posterior density plots for key parameters. Report percent deviation from the reference specification. At N=15-20, expect visible sensitivity; the goal is showing conclusions are qualitatively stable, not numerically identical.

## Issue 2: Bilinear Identifiability and the Ablation

**The reviewer is correct that eta_i will be heavily shrunk.** With 15-20 binary observations per item, individual eta_i estimates will be dominated by the hierarchical prior. [Konig & Alexandrowicz (2024)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10846471/) show that in hierarchical Bayesian IRT, individual parameters shrink toward the grand mean as effective sample size decreases. With only 15-20 observations per eta_i, these are essentially unidentifiable individually ("pre-asymptotically non-identifiable").

**How to quantify shrinkage:** Compare each eta_i posterior to the hierarchical prior. If the posterior SD is barely narrower than the prior SD, the data contribute almost no information. Report the ratio `prior_SD / posterior_SD` -- values near 1.0 confirm prior dominance. Also report the effective shrinkage: `(eta_i_posterior_mean - prior_mean) / (eta_i_MLE - prior_mean)` where values near 0 mean total shrinkage to the prior.

**The ablation is well-motivated.** The DGM literature (Shu, Leucht, & Henson, 2013; discussed on [Stan Forums](https://discourse.mc-stan.org/t/syntax-for-irt-model-for-detecting-cheating/4152)) uses person-level cheating parameters with item status treated as known or estimated separately -- effectively a xi_j-only model. If it does, the hierarchical eta_i still has value as a population-level summary even if individual estimates are shrunk.

**Key recommendation:** Frame eta_i not as individually identified parameters but as contributing to a better-estimated population-level hyperparameter (the distribution of item susceptibility), which regularizes xi_j estimates.

**IRT Simulation Study Research Findings for Gated 2PL with N=15-20**

The practical recommendation: start with 100; verify stability by running a subset at 150. For Bayesian MCMC models, 50-100 replications is defensible if each replication is expensive.
- **Metrics:** The standard set is **bias**, **RMSE**, and **correlation** between true and estimated parameters. Many studies also report **coverage rates** of 95% credible intervals and **interval length**. Convergence rate is critical for small-N conditions.
- **Factors varied:** Sample size (N), test length (number of items), and parameter distributions (discrimination/difficulty ranges). A fully crossed design is standard.

**2. Minimum Viable N for 2PL Recovery**

The literature floor is **N=50**, not lower. Key evidence:
- Konig et al. (2020/2023) tested N=50, 75, 100, 150, 200, 500 with an optimized hierarchical Bayesian 2PL. At N=50, MML had 75-89% inadmissible solutions; hierarchical Bayes succeeded but with elevated RMSE.
- HBMIRT (2024) tested N=50, 100, 500. Hierarchical priors produced minimal bias at N=50 (bias=0.050 for slopes vs. 0.215 for ML). All Bayesian runs converged at N=50.
- Fox (2025, JEBS) IRT-BCSM integrates out person parameters and works at N=50-100, but was **not tested below N=50**.
- de la Torre & Hong (2010) used hierarchical Bayesian higher-order IRT for small samples but studied item calibration, not examinee counts as low as 15-20.
- **No published study was found that recovers standard 2PL parameters at N<50.** At N=25, convergence failures are documented as frequent.

**3. Bilinear/Multiplicative Interaction Parameters**

No simulation study was found specifically addressing parameter recovery for bilinear/multiplicative interaction terms (like your gating parameter product) in an IRT framework. This is a gap. The identifiability literature on multiplicative latent factor models warns that such terms face severe identifiability challenges with few observations, compounded at small N. You would be contributing novel methodology here, which strengthens the case for a simulation study but also means there is no established benchmark to cite.

**4. IRT with LLMs as Examinees (<30)**

IRT-Router used 20 LLMs but performed no parameter recovery study and did not acknowledge the small-N issue. Most IRT-for-LLM papers (tinyBenchmarks, Latency-Response Theory) treat items as the estimation target and LLMs as fixed, sidestepping person-parameter recovery. No paper was found doing rigorous IRT parameter recovery validation at N=15-20 examinees.

- Run **100 replications** minimum (50 acceptable if computation is prohibitive; justify with stability analysis).
